# 5. Split by Person

```{r repeated-measures}
days_per_person <- table(days$id)
summary(as.vector(days_per_person))

# share of life satisfaction variance between people (one-way ANOVA ICC)
aov_fit <- anova(lm(life_satisfaction ~ factor(id), data = days))
ms_b  <- aov_fit["factor(id)", "Mean Sq"]
ms_w  <- aov_fit["Residuals", "Mean Sq"]
k_avg <- (nrow(days) - sum(days_per_person^2) / nrow(days)) / (length(days_per_person) - 1)
icc   <- (ms_b - ms_w) / (ms_b + (k_avg - 1) * ms_w)
round(icc, 2)
```

About `r round(100 * icc)`% of the variation in daily life satisfaction lies
between people. The intake predictors are also constant within a person. A
split over days would put most people in both sets. A model could then learn
each person's usual level from their training days, partly through the intake
variables, and score well on the test set without predicting anything new.

So we depart from the handout's day-level `initial_split()`, as the proposal
says, and split by **person**:

- `group_initial_split()` puts 70% of people in the training set and 30% in
  the test set, with seed 559.
- The split is stratified on each person's mean life satisfaction (quartiles).
  This is the person-level version of "stratified on the target."
- Cross-validation also holds out whole people.

The test set therefore checks how well the model does for **new players**.

```{r split}
person_ls <- tapply(days$life_satisfaction, days$id, mean)
days$ls_strata <- cut(person_ls[as.character(days$id)],
                      breaks = quantile(person_ls, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.25)),
                      include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)

set.seed(559)
split <- group_initial_split(days, group = id, prop = 0.7, strata = ls_strata)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

split_sizes <- data.frame(
  set    = c("training", "test"),
  days   = c(nrow(train), nrow(test)),
  people = c(n_distinct(train$id), n_distinct(test$id)),
  mean_life_sat = round(c(mean(train$life_satisfaction), mean(test$life_satisfaction)), 1),
  sd_life_sat   = round(c(sd(train$life_satisfaction), sd(test$life_satisfaction)), 1))
split_sizes

# no person is in both sets
length(intersect(train$id, test$id))
```

From here on, `test` is used only to receive the cluster labels and component
scores learned on `train`, until the final evaluation in Section 9.

```{r folds}
n_folds <- 10

set.seed(559)
folds <- groupKFold(train$id, k = n_folds)

# The folds are fit in parallel (Section 8), so set.seed() alone would not
# fix the random parts of each fit (the forests' bootstrap samples).
# caret takes one seed per fold and tuning value, plus one for the final fit.
# 1000 per fold covers every tuning grid used here.
fold_seeds <- c(lapply(seq_len(n_folds), function(i) sample.int(1e6, 1000)),
                list(sample.int(1e6, 1)))
ctrl  <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = n_folds, index = folds,
                      savePredictions = "final", seeds = fold_seeds)

# people and days held out in each fold
sapply(folds, function(rows) c(people_out = n_distinct(train$id[-rows]),
                               days_out   = nrow(train) - length(rows)))
```

The handout asks us to state the number of folds. We use **`r n_folds`
grouped folds**, the number the handout asks for in the report ("use ten in
your report"). Each fold holds out
about a tenth of the training people.
All models (Section 8) get these same folds through `index`.

# 6. Unsupervised Analysis

Everything in this section is fit on the **training days only**. Test days
get their cluster labels and component scores from the training fit.
Neither block contains the target. Both are imputed (training medians) and
centered and scaled (training means and SDs) in a recipe first, because
K-means and PCA work from distances and cannot take missing values. Both
blocks are 1 to 7 numeric items, so there are no categorical items to
encode.

**Why the blocks are filled with the median here, but with KNN in the
models.**

- **The blocks must be filled first.** K-means and PCA cannot run with
  missing values, and they are run once, here, before any model.
- **KNN has nothing to work with inside a block.** KNN fills a missing
  answer by finding days with similar answers to the other questions. But a
  day missing one item of a block is missing all six (Section 4), so within
  the block there are no other answers to compare. The training median is
  the simple fill that is left.
- **The models are different.** Their recipes (Section 8) see every
  predictor, so KNN has plenty to match on there, and caret relearns it in
  each fold.
- **No leakage.** The medians come from the training days only and never
  use the target.
- **Small cost.** Every filled day gets the same values: the same play-day
  type and the same two component scores (shown below). Only
  `r sum(rowSums(is.na(train[bangs])) > 0)` training and
  `r sum(rowSums(is.na(test[bangs])) > 0)` test days are filled for the
  BANGS items, and `r sum(rowSums(is.na(train[needs])) > 0)` training and
  `r sum(rowSums(is.na(test[needs])) > 0)` test days for the needs items.
  The effect on the structure and on set B is negligible.

## 6a. Clustering: types of play days

The handout asks for clusters that are types of days. Each play day is
clustered on its six BANGS answers, which describe how that day's most
recent gaming session went, so each type is a kind of play day defined by
its gaming. Days without play have no BANGS answers and no type.

### The block

```{r bangs-recipe}
rec_bangs <- recipe(~ ., data = train[bangs]) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  prep()

train_bangs <- bake(rec_bangs, new_data = train)
test_bangs  <- bake(rec_bangs, new_data = test)

round(cor(train_bangs), 2)
```

Autonomy and progress go together, and wishing to do something else,
disappointment, and toxicity go together. Forming relationships is nearly
independent of the rest.

### How many types?

We use two criteria: the **elbow** in the total within-cluster sum of
squares, and the **average silhouette width**. Each K-means fit uses 25
random starts. The silhouette is computed from the distances between all
training days.

```{r choose-k}
k_range <- 1:8

km_fits <- lapply(k_range, function(k) {
  set.seed(559)
  kmeans(train_bangs, centers = k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 50)
})

bangs_dist <- dist(train_bangs)
k_choice <- data.frame(
  K   = k_range,
  wss = sapply(km_fits, `[[`, "tot.withinss"),
  silhouette = c(NA, sapply(km_fits[-1], function(km)
    mean(silhouette(km$cluster, bangs_dist)[, 3]))))
rm(bangs_dist)

k_choice %>% mutate(share_of_k1 = round(wss / wss[1], 3),
                    silhouette  = round(silhouette, 3))
```

```{r elbow-plot, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Elbow plot: total within-cluster sum of squares by K (training days)."}
ggplot(k_choice, aes(K, wss)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = k_range) +
  labs(y = "Total within-cluster sum of squares")
```

```{r silhouette-plot, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Average silhouette width by K (training days)."}
ggplot(filter(k_choice, K > 1), aes(K, silhouette)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = k_range) +
  labs(y = "Average silhouette width")
```

**Choosing K.** Both criteria point to the same region, and neither gives a
sharp answer:

- The silhouette is highest at K = 2
  (`r round(k_choice$silhouette[2], 2)`). It is
  `r round(k_choice$silhouette[3], 2)` at K = 3 and stays near that value
  for every larger K. Silhouettes around 0.2 to 0.3 mean the types overlap.
  Play days vary continuously and do not fall into separate groups.
- The elbow bends at K = 2 to 3. Going from 1 to 2 clusters removes
  `r round(100 * (1 - k_choice$wss[2] / k_choice$wss[1]))`% of the
  within-cluster variation, 2 to 3 removes another
  `r round(100 * (k_choice$wss[2] - k_choice$wss[3]) / k_choice$wss[1])`%,
  and later steps remove less.

We keep **K = 3**:

- **Against K = 2.** K = 2 only separates good play days from bad ones.
  K = 3 splits the good days by whether the person formed relationships
  while playing. That is the one BANGS item the others do not capture (the
  correlation table above), and the split matters for the target (below).
- **Against K = 4.** K = 4 is a finer cut. It splits the frustrating days
  further, but its silhouette is no better and the solution is less stable.
- Section 8 checks K = 2 and K = 4 against K = 3 on the training folds:
  profiles, stability, and prediction.

```{r k-final}
k_final <- 3
km <- km_fits[[k_final]]

km$size
round(km$betweenss / km$totss, 2)   # share of variation between the clusters
```

### Profiles and names

The centroids are in z scores. The profile table gives the item means in the
original 1 to 7 units, the cluster sizes, and who the person played with.

```{r cluster-profiles}
cluster_profile <- function(labels) {
  train[bangs] %>%
    mutate(cluster = labels) %>%
    group_by(cluster) %>%
    summarise(across(everything(), ~ round(mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), 1)),
              days = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
    as.data.frame()
}

cluster_profile(km_fits[[2]]$cluster)   # K = 2, for comparison
cluster_profile(km$cluster)
```

The names are assigned by rule, so they stay attached to the right cluster
even if the cluster numbers change:

- the cluster with the highest relationships mean is the **connected play
  day**;
- of the other two, the one with lower autonomy is the **frustrating play
  day**;
- the last is the **smooth solo play day**.

```{r cluster-names}
prof <- cluster_profile(km$cluster)
connected   <- prof$cluster[which.max(prof$gaming_relationships)]
others      <- setdiff(prof$cluster, connected)
frustrating <- others[which.min(prof$gaming_autonomy[match(others, prof$cluster)])]
smooth      <- setdiff(others, c(frustrating))

cluster_names <- character(k_final)
cluster_names[connected]   <- "Connected play day"
cluster_names[frustrating] <- "Frustrating play day"
cluster_names[smooth]      <- "Smooth solo play day"

type_levels <- c("Smooth solo play day", "Connected play day", "Frustrating play day")
train$play_day_type <- factor(cluster_names[km$cluster], levels = type_levels)

table(train$play_day_type)
```

```{r cluster-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Cluster centroids on the six BANGS items (z scores, training days)."}
as.data.frame(km$centers) %>%
  mutate(cluster = paste0(cluster_names, " (n = ", km$size, ")")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cluster, names_to = "item", values_to = "z") %>%
  mutate(item = sub("gaming_", "", item)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(item, z, fill = item)) +
  geom_col() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ cluster) + coord_flip() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cluster mean (z score)")
```

Who people played with, and what they played, in each type (row
percentages, training days):

```{r cluster-context}
round(100 * prop.table(table(train$play_day_type, train$play_context), 1))
round(100 * prop.table(table(train$play_day_type, train$game_type), 1))
```

What the three types are:

- **Smooth solo play day.** The person played the way they wanted and made
  progress. There was little disappointment and almost no toxicity, but no
  relationships were formed. Most of these days were solo, single-player
  play.
- **Connected play day.** The gaming went just as smoothly, and the person
  also formed relationships with other players or characters. These days are
  split between solo and friends play. The item asks about players *or
  characters*, so a story game can count.
- **Frustrating play day.** Autonomy and progress were lower, and wishing to
  do something else, disappointment, and toxicity were higher. Team
  competition and strangers-only play are more common than on the other
  types of day.

Compared with the proposal: the expected day with a "satisfying solo
session" appears. The days with a "toxic competitive" or "low improvement"
session appear together as one frustrating type, which leans toward
competitive play but is not defined by it. Toxicity is only moderate even there (mean
`r prof$gaming_toxic[frustrating]` on the 1 to 7 scale, below the midpoint).
At K = 4 the two separate (Section 8), but the extra split is less stable
and is not supported by the silhouette.

### Life satisfaction across the types (training days)

```{r target-by-cluster}
train %>%
  group_by(play_day_type) %>%
  summarise(days = n(),
            mean_life_sat = round(mean(life_satisfaction), 1),
            sd_life_sat   = round(sd(life_satisfaction), 1),
            pct_stress    = round(100 * mean(had_stress == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            mean_sleep    = round(mean(sleep_quality, na.rm = TRUE), 2)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

```{r target-by-cluster-plot, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Life satisfaction by type of play day (training days)."}
ggplot(train, aes(play_day_type, life_satisfaction, fill = play_day_type)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Life satisfaction today (0 to 100)")
```

The type of play day is clearly related to life satisfaction that day, even
though no BANGS item asks about life. Frustrating play days are the lowest
and connected play days the highest. The spread within each type is wide,
and these are same-day associations. A bad day may make the gaming feel
worse as much as the other way around.

### Test days

`kmeans()` has no `predict()` method. A test day joins the training centroid
it is closest to, in the training-standardized units.

```{r assign-test}
nearest_centroid <- function(x, centers) {
  x  <- as.matrix(x)
  d2 <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(centers)), function(k)
    rowSums((x - matrix(centers[k, ], nrow(x), ncol(x), byrow = TRUE))^2))
  max.col(-d2, ties.method = "first")
}

test$play_day_type <- factor(cluster_names[nearest_centroid(test_bangs, km$centers)],
                            levels = type_levels)

# the rule gives the training days their own clusters back
mean(nearest_centroid(train_bangs, km$centers) == km$cluster)

round(rbind(train = prop.table(table(train$play_day_type)),
            test  = prop.table(table(test$play_day_type))), 2)

# days with no BANGS answers were filled with the training medians, so they
# all get the play-day type nearest the median profile
table(filled_day_type = c(
  as.character(train$play_day_type[rowSums(is.na(train[bangs])) > 0]),
  as.character(test$play_day_type[rowSums(is.na(test[bangs])) > 0])))
```

## 6b. Principal components: dimensions of a day's needs

### The block

```{r needs-recipe}
rec_needs <- recipe(~ ., data = train[needs]) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  prep()

train_needs <- bake(rec_needs, new_data = train)
test_needs  <- bake(rec_needs, new_data = test)

round(cor(train_needs), 2)
```

```{r pca}
pca <- prcomp(train_needs, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca)
```

### How many components?

We use the three rules from the PCA lecture, parallel analysis (one of the
criteria the handout lists), and theory:

- **The scree plot.** Keep the components before the curve flattens.
- **The eigenvalue rule.** A component's eigenvalue is its variance. Each
  standardized item has a variance of 1, so a component with an eigenvalue
  of 1 or more explains more than a single item does. The lecture uses 1 as
  the cutoff and the walkthrough's code uses 0.75, so both are shown.
- **Cumulative variance.** Keep enough components to explain 80% of the
  variance.
- **Parallel analysis.** Run PCA on 100 sets of random, uncorrelated data of
  the same size (`r nrow(train_needs)` days by `r length(needs)` items).
  Keep a component only if its eigenvalue beats the 95th percentile of the
  random eigenvalues at the same position, so it holds more than chance
  alone would give.
- **Theory.** What the items were written to measure.

```{r n-components}
eig <- pca$sdev^2
pve <- eig / sum(eig)

# parallel analysis: eigenvalues of random data with the same rows and columns
set.seed(559)
random_eig <- replicate(100, prcomp(matrix(rnorm(nrow(train_needs) * length(needs)),
                                           ncol = length(needs)), scale. = TRUE)$sdev^2)
pa_cut <- apply(random_eig, 1, quantile, 0.95)

n_comp_rules <- data.frame(PC = seq_along(eig), eigenvalue = round(eig, 2),
                           pve = round(pve, 3), cumulative = round(cumsum(pve), 3),
                           random_95 = round(pa_cut, 3))
n_comp_rules

# components each rule keeps (eigenvalues fall in order, so a count works)
c(eigenvalue_1      = sum(eig >= 1),
  eigenvalue_0.75   = sum(eig >= 0.75),
  cumulative_80     = which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.80)[1],
  parallel_analysis = sum(eig > pa_cut))
```

```{r scree-plot, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Scree plot: proportion of variance explained by each component of the six needs items (training days). The dashed line is the parallel-analysis cutoff on the same scale."}
ggplot(n_comp_rules, aes(PC, pve)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() +
  geom_line(aes(y = random_95 / length(needs)), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_along(eig)) +
  labs(y = "Proportion of variance explained")
```

**Choosing the number.** The rules disagree, which the lecture notes is
normal:

| Rule | Components kept |
|---|---|
| Scree plot | 1: the curve drops steeply from component 1 to 2 (`r round(100 * pve[1], 1)`% to `r round(100 * pve[2], 1)`%) and flattens after that |
| Eigenvalue of 1 or more (lecture) | `r sum(eig >= 1)` |
| Eigenvalue of 0.75 or more (walkthrough) | `r sum(eig >= 0.75)` (the second eigenvalue is `r round(eig[2], 2)`) |
| 80% of the variance | `r which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.80)[1]` (two components explain `r round(100 * cumsum(pve)[2], 1)`%, three `r round(100 * cumsum(pve)[3], 1)`%) |
| Parallel analysis | `r sum(eig > pa_cut)` (the second eigenvalue, `r round(eig[2], 2)`, is below the random cutoff of `r round(pa_cut[2], 2)`) |
| Theory (self-determination theory) | 2: need satisfaction and need frustration |

Parallel analysis and the eigenvalue rule at 1 agree here, and with this
much data they are close to the same test, so they count as one piece of
evidence rather than two. Parallel analysis replaces the fixed cutoff of 1
with the eigenvalues of random data, which stray from 1 only by chance. With
`r nrow(train_needs)` days and `r length(needs)` items they barely stray (the
cutoff for the second component is `r round(pa_cut[2], 2)`). The two rules
part ways only when the sample is small or the items are many.

- **The case for one.** The first component alone explains
  `r round(100 * pve[1])`% of the variance. It is a general "good day for my
  needs" dimension, with every satisfaction item positive and every
  frustration item negative.
- **We keep two**, as theory and the walkthrough's cutoff say.
  Self-determination theory treats satisfaction and frustration as separate
  experiences, and the proposal predicted exactly these two dimensions. Two
  components also carry more of the frustration items, which the first
  component carries less well.
- **Section 8 checks** one and three components (the 80% rule's choice)
  against two on the training folds.

```{r loadings}
n_keep <- 2

loadings <- pca$rotation[, 1:n_keep] %*% diag(pca$sdev[1:n_keep])
colnames(loadings) <- paste0("PC", 1:n_keep)
round(loadings, 2)
```

### Rotation and names

The unrotated pair is one general component plus a contrast, which is hard to
name. A varimax rotation turns the two axes within the same plane. The
variance they explain together does not change.

```{r rotate}
rotation <- varimax(loadings)
rotated  <- unclass(rotation$loadings)
colnames(rotated) <- paste0("RC", 1:n_keep)

# flip each component so its strongest items load positively
flip <- sign(apply(rotated, 2, function(l) l[which.max(abs(l))]))
rotated <- sweep(rotated, 2, flip, "*")

# name each component by which kind of item it carries
sat_items  <- grepl("_satisfied$", rownames(rotated))
is_sat     <- colMeans(abs(rotated[sat_items, ])) > colMeans(abs(rotated[!sat_items, ]))
comp_names <- unname(ifelse(is_sat, "need_satisfaction", "need_frustration"))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(comp_names))
colnames(rotated) <- comp_names

round(rotated, 2)

# variance explained by the two rotated components together
round(sum(rotated^2) / length(needs), 3)
```

```{r loadings-plot, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Rotated loadings of the six needs items on the two components."}
as.data.frame(rotated) %>%
  mutate(item = factor(sub("needs_", "", rownames(rotated)),
                       levels = rev(sub("needs_", "", rownames(rotated))))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-item, names_to = "component", values_to = "loading") %>%
  ggplot(aes(component, item, fill = loading)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", loading)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

- **Need satisfaction.** The three satisfaction items (autonomy, competence,
  relatedness) load highly. A high score is a day the person did what they
  valued, did it well, and felt close to people.
- **Need frustration.** The three frustration items load highly (after the
  flip). A high score is a day the person felt forced, insecure, or
  excluded. Competence frustration loads on both components.

### Compared with the proposal

The proposal expected two components, one for general satisfaction and one
for general frustration, rather than one for each need. It read that result
as days differing "more in how fulfilling or frustrating they are overall
rather than in which specific need is met." Two numbers help check that
reading: how strongly the satisfied and frustrated items go together, and
what a third component would hold.

```{r needs-vs-proposal}
needs_cor <- cor(train_needs)
sat <- grepl("_satisfied$", needs)

# correlations between each satisfied item and each frustrated item
round(range(needs_cor[sat, !sat]), 2)

# three varimax-rotated components; the one that carries relatedness
# frustration most, flipped so that item loads positively (Section 8 tests
# whether a third component helps prediction)
L3 <- unclass(varimax(pca$rotation[, 1:3] %*% diag(pca$sdev[1:3]))$loadings)
rel_comp <- which.max(abs(L3["needs_relatedness_frustrated", ]))
third <- L3[, rel_comp] * sign(L3["needs_relatedness_frustrated", rel_comp])
round(third, 2)
```

- **What matches.** The two rotated components are need satisfaction and
  need frustration, as predicted. Each item loads mainly on its own side, and
  neither component belongs to a single need.
- **Satisfaction and frustration go together.** The first unrotated
  component alone explains `r round(100 * pve[1])`% of the variance, and
  every satisfied item correlates between
  `r round(min(needs_cor[sat, !sat]), 2)` and
  `r round(max(needs_cor[sat, !sat]), 2)` with every frustrated item. A day
  that meets a person's needs is usually also a day low in frustration. The
  two rotated scores are uncorrelated only because varimax keeps the axes at
  right angles. That is a property of the method, not a finding.
- **One need partly stands apart: relatedness.** A third component, the one
  the 80% rule would keep, is mostly relatedness: relatedness frustration
  loads `r round(third[["needs_relatedness_frustrated"]], 2)` and relatedness
  satisfaction `r round(third[["needs_relatedness_satisfied"]], 2)`. It is
  small (eigenvalue `r round(eig[3], 2)`, `r round(100 * pve[3], 1)`% of the
  variance), and Section 8 shows it adds nothing to predicting life
  satisfaction. Autonomy and competence cannot be told apart: their
  satisfaction items correlate
  `r round(needs_cor["needs_autonomy_satisfied", "needs_competence_satisfied"], 2)`.
- **Days and people.** The components are fit on days pooled across people,
  so they mix differences between people with differences between one
  person's days. A high need-satisfaction score marks a good day partly
  because it marks a person whose days usually go well.

The proposal's reading holds, with one qualification: the days differ mostly
in how fulfilling they are overall, but relatedness carries a little variance
of its own. These components are **dimensions** of a day. The **types** of
days come from the clustering in Section 6a.

### Scores for every day

Test scores use the training weights, the training SDs, and the same rotation
and flip.

```{r scores}
component_scores <- function(block) {
  raw <- predict(pca, newdata = block)[, 1:n_keep, drop = FALSE]
  standardized <- sweep(raw, 2, pca$sdev[1:n_keep], "/")
  out <- sweep(standardized %*% rotation$rotmat, 2, flip, "*")
  colnames(out) <- comp_names
  out
}

train <- bind_cols(train, as.data.frame(component_scores(train_needs)))
test  <- bind_cols(test,  as.data.frame(component_scores(test_needs)))

round(rbind(train_mean = colMeans(train[comp_names]),
            train_sd   = sapply(train[comp_names], sd),
            test_mean  = colMeans(test[comp_names])), 2)

# days with no needs answers were filled with the training medians, so they
# all get the same two scores
unique(round(as.data.frame(train)[rowSums(is.na(train[needs])) > 0, comp_names], 2))
```

### Components, clusters, and the target (training days)

```{r comp-cluster}
train %>%
  group_by(play_day_type) %>%
  summarise(days = n(), across(all_of(comp_names), ~ round(mean(.x), 2))) %>%
  as.data.frame()

round(cor(train[c(comp_names, "life_satisfaction")]), 2)
```

Need satisfaction is strongly related to life satisfaction on the same day.
That is expected, and Section 7 discusses what it means for the model. Need
frustration is related more weakly, and in the opposite direction. The
play-day types line up with the components: frustrating play days are
lower on need satisfaction and higher on need frustration. The two blocks
describe overlapping but different parts of the day.

# 7. Feature Sets and Leakage

## Feature sets A and B

Both sets share every predictor that is not in the needs block, including the
six BANGS items:

- **Set A** adds the six needs items.
- **Set B** replaces the six needs items with their two component scores and
  adds the play-day type (the cluster) as a factor, as the handout defines
  set B.

The clustering block is a chosen set of predictors (the BANGS items), not the
PCA block, as the handout allows. So the BANGS items stay in both sets, and
the A versus B comparison asks two things. Do two scores carry what the six
needs items carry? Does the play-day type add anything to the items it was
built from?

```{r feature-sets}
shared <- c(bangs, day_preds, person_preds)
set_A  <- c(shared, needs)
set_B  <- c(shared, comp_names, "play_day_type")

c(A = length(set_A), B = length(set_B))
setdiff(set_A, set_B)
setdiff(set_B, set_A)

train_A <- train[c("life_satisfaction", set_A)]
train_B <- train[c("life_satisfaction", set_B)]
test_A  <- test[c("life_satisfaction", set_A)]
test_B  <- test[c("life_satisfaction", set_B)]
```

## Data leakage we considered

- **The target in another form.** Affective valence (r =
  `r round(cor(raw$affective_valence, raw$life_satisfaction, use = "complete.obs"), 2)`
  with life satisfaction) was removed.
  - The needs items are kept, as the proposal planned. They ask about the
    day's experiences (doing what one values, feeling close to people), not
    about satisfaction with life. But they are answered in the same sitting,
    and need satisfaction correlates
    `r round(cor(train$need_satisfaction, train$life_satisfaction), 2)` with
    the target. Much of the model's accuracy will come from them, and that
    accuracy describes what goes together on a day. It does not show that
    needs cause life satisfaction.
  - No block contains the target, so no cluster or component is built from
    it.
- **Lags.** Every daily predictor is from the same day, so there is no lag
  that could reach forward into the next day.
- **Repeated measures.** The split and the folds hold out whole people
  (Section 5).
- **Preprocessing.** Imputation, dummy coding, and scaling are in recipes,
  re-learned inside each fold. The recoding in Section 3 learns nothing from
  the data.
- **Unsupervised structure.** The clusters and components were fit on the
  training days only, and the test days were scored from that fit.
  - One smaller issue remains inside cross-validation. The cluster
    centroids, the component weights, and the medians that fill the blocks
    were learned from all training days, so in each fold the held-out days
    helped shape them.
  - The structure never uses the target, and six items fit on about 8,700
    days barely move when a tenth of them are held out. So the effect on the
    cross-validated comparison should be negligible.
  - The test set is untouched by this.
- **Information from the future.** The intake survey must come before the
  diary days it describes:

```{r intake-timing}
intake_time <- as.POSIXct(train$intake_date, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")
gap_days    <- as.numeric(difftime(train$date, intake_time, units = "days"))
summary(gap_days)
c(diary_days_before_intake = sum(gap_days < 0, na.rm = TRUE))
```

# 8. Supervised Models

## Recipes

```{r recipes}
# regularized regression: dummy columns and standardized predictors
recipe_linear <- function(dat) {
  recipe(life_satisfaction ~ ., data = dat) %>%
    step_impute_median(age, education) %>%
    step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = 5) %>%
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
    step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
}

# trees: the same imputation, factors kept whole, no scaling
recipe_tree <- function(dat) {
  recipe(life_satisfaction ~ ., data = dat) %>%
    step_impute_median(age, education) %>%
    step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = 5) %>%
    step_zv(all_predictors())
}

rec <- list(linear_A = recipe_linear(train_A), linear_B = recipe_linear(train_B),
            tree_A   = recipe_tree(train_A),   tree_B   = recipe_tree(train_B))

# prep once to check the recipes and count the columns each model sees
baked <- lapply(rec, function(r) bake(prep(r), new_data = NULL))
sapply(baked, function(b) c(columns = ncol(b) - 1, missing_left = sum(is.na(b))))
```

- **Imputation.** Age and education get the training median, because they
  are constant within a person. Everything else is imputed with five nearest
  neighbors, never using the target.
- **The ordered stressor factor** becomes polynomial contrasts for the
  elastic net. The trees split it only between neighboring levels.
- **The trees** do not need dummy columns or scaling.

## Models and tuning grids

The handout requires a null model, a regularized regression with `glmnet`,
and a tree ensemble. As in the course walkthrough, we fit the null model,
the elastic net, and the random forest, on both feature sets, with the same
`r n_folds` grouped folds and the same seeds.
The folds are fit in parallel, so the random parts of each fit are fixed by
the seeds list in `trainControl()` (Section 5), which is drawn from
`set.seed(559)`.

**Reproducibility.** We checked this by refitting. The null model, both
elastic nets, both random forests, and every check in this section
reproduce exactly.

| Model | `method` | Tuning grid |
|---|---|---|
| Null (training mean) | `"null"` | none; it uses no predictors, so it is fit once |
| Elastic net | `"glmnet"` | `alpha` 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 (0 is ridge, 1 is the lasso) × 60 `lambda` values, log-spaced from 10^-4 × to 10 × the smallest lambda that zeroes every coefficient |
| Random forest | `"ranger"` | `mtry` 2, √p, p/3, p/2, p (rounded, p = predictor count of that set) × `min.node.size` 5, 20, 50, 100, 200; `splitrule = "variance"`; 500 trees; impurity importance; `respect.unordered.factors = "order"`, so an unordered factor's levels are sorted by their mean life satisfaction before each split (ranger's default would split them in their stored order). The first run used `mtry` up to p/2 and `min.node.size` 5, 20, 50. The best values were at the top edge (node size 50 for both sets, `mtry` p/2 for set B), so p, 100, and 200 were added |

A helper reports whether each best tuning value is inside its grid or at an
edge. A best value at an edge would mean the grid should be widened.

```{r edge-helper}
edge_check <- function(fit) {
  sapply(names(fit$bestTune), function(v) {
    vals <- sort(unique(fit$results[[v]]))
    b    <- fit$bestTune[[v]]
    if (length(vals) == 1) "fixed"
    else if (b == min(vals)) "lowest value tried"
    else if (b == max(vals)) "highest value tried"
    else "interior"
  })
}

# fit a model, or read the saved fit. set.seed(559) stays right before each
# train() call, as in the walkthrough; the seeds in `ctrl` are what fix the
# parallel fits
fit_dir <- out_path("model_fits")
dir.create(fit_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

# The recipe's column selectors keep a link to the R session they were made
# in, so a saved fit can carry a copy of every object in the session (over
# 100 MB a file). Pointing them at the global environment before saving keeps
# each file small. Nothing after the fit uses that link: the cross-validated
# results and the predictions are unchanged.
drop_session <- function(x) {
  if (rlang::is_quosure(x)) return(rlang::quo_set_env(x, globalenv()))
  if (is.list(x) && !is.data.frame(x)) {
    a <- attributes(x)
    x <- lapply(x, drop_session)
    attributes(x) <- a
  }
  x
}

fit_or_load <- function(name, expr) {
  file <- file.path(fit_dir, paste0(name, ".rds"))
  if (!refit_models && file.exists(file)) return(readRDS(file))
  fit <- expr                       # evaluated here, so the fit runs only when needed
  fit$recipe$steps <- lapply(fit$recipe$steps, drop_session)
  saveRDS(fit, file)
  fit
}

# fit the folds in parallel: caret sends each fold to its own R worker. The
# seeds in `ctrl` (drawn from set.seed(559)) fix the random parts of each
# fit whatever the number of cores. Two cores
# are left free for the rest of the computer.
n_workers <- max(1, min(n_folds, parallel::detectCores() - 2))
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(n_workers)
registerDoParallel(cl)
```

## Null model

```{r fit-null}
fit_null <- fit_or_load("null", {
  set.seed(559)
  train(rec$linear_A, data = train_A, method = "null", trControl = ctrl)
})
getTrainPerf(fit_null)
```

## Elastic net

```{r fit-glmnet}
lambda_grid <- function(b) {
  x <- as.matrix(b[names(b) != "life_satisfaction"])
  lambda_max <- max(glmnet(x, b$life_satisfaction, alpha = 1)$lambda)
  10^seq(log10(lambda_max) - 4, log10(lambda_max) + 1, length.out = 60)
}

fit_glmnet_A <- fit_or_load("glmnet_A", {
  set.seed(559)
  train(rec$linear_A, data = train_A, method = "glmnet", trControl = ctrl,
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
                               lambda = lambda_grid(baked$linear_A)))
})
fit_glmnet_B <- fit_or_load("glmnet_B", {
  set.seed(559)
  train(rec$linear_B, data = train_B, method = "glmnet", trControl = ctrl,
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
                               lambda = lambda_grid(baked$linear_B)))
})

rbind(A = cbind(fit_glmnet_A$bestTune, t(edge_check(fit_glmnet_A))),
      B = cbind(fit_glmnet_B$bestTune, t(edge_check(fit_glmnet_B))))
```

```{r glmnet-plot, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Elastic net: cross-validated RMSE across lambda, one line per alpha (feature set A)."}
ggplot(fit_glmnet_A) + scale_x_log10()
```

## Random forest

```{r fit-rf}
# widened after the first run (see the table above): p added to mtry, and
# 100 and 200 added to min.node.size
rf_grid <- function(p) {
  expand.grid(mtry = sort(unique(pmax(2, round(c(2, sqrt(p), p / 3, p / 2, p))))),
              splitrule = "variance",
              min.node.size = c(5, 20, 50, 100, 200))
}
p_A <- ncol(baked$tree_A) - 1
p_B <- ncol(baked$tree_B) - 1

fit_rf_A <- fit_or_load("rf_A", {
  set.seed(559)
  train(rec$tree_A, data = train_A, method = "ranger", trControl = ctrl,
        tuneGrid = rf_grid(p_A), num.trees = 500, importance = "impurity",
        respect.unordered.factors = "order",
        num.threads = 1)   # one thread per fold; the folds already run in parallel
})
fit_rf_B <- fit_or_load("rf_B", {
  set.seed(559)
  train(rec$tree_B, data = train_B, method = "ranger", trControl = ctrl,
        tuneGrid = rf_grid(p_B), num.trees = 500, importance = "impurity",
        respect.unordered.factors = "order",
        num.threads = 1)
})

rbind(A = cbind(fit_rf_A$bestTune, t(edge_check(fit_rf_A))),
      B = cbind(fit_rf_B$bestTune, t(edge_check(fit_rf_B))))
```

```{r rf-plot, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Random forest: cross-validated RMSE across mtry and minimum node size (feature set A)."}
ggplot(fit_rf_A)
```

**Edges.** The edge labels in the tables above show whether each best tuning
value was inside its grid. Both elastic nets' best `alpha` and `lambda` are
inside the grid.

```{r rf-edge}
# set A's forest at its best mtry, across node sizes (used below)
rf_A_nodes <- filter(fit_rf_A$results, mtry == fit_rf_A$bestTune$mtry)
```

**The random forest.** Its grid was widened after the first run's best
values landed on the top edge (see the grid table).

- Set B's best values are inside the wider grid: `mtry` =
  `r fit_rf_B$bestTune$mtry` with node size
  `r fit_rf_B$bestTune$min.node.size`.
- Set A's best node size is now `r fit_rf_A$bestTune$min.node.size`, the
  bottom of the grid and ranger's default for regression (with `mtry` =
  `r fit_rf_A$bestTune$mtry`).
- At that `mtry`, the RMSE barely changes from node size 5 to 50
  (`r paste(round(range(rf_A_nodes$RMSE[rf_A_nodes$min.node.size <= 50]), 3), collapse = " to ")`).
  Set A's best forest is
  `r round(min(fit_rf_A$results$RMSE) - min(fit_glmnet_B$results$RMSE), 2)`
  RMSE behind the best elastic net, so smaller nodes would not change the
  ranking.

## The cross-validated comparison

Every model used the same folds, so `resamples()` lines them up fold by fold.

```{r resamples}
fits <- list(null = fit_null,
             glmnet_A = fit_glmnet_A, glmnet_B = fit_glmnet_B,
             rf_A = fit_rf_A, rf_B = fit_rf_B)

model_label <- c(null = "Null", glmnet = "Elastic net", rf = "Random forest")

results_cv <- resamples(fits)
summary(results_cv)$statistics$RMSE |> round(3)
```

The table the report needs: one row per model and feature set, with the
mean over the folds and the fold-to-fold spread (SD) of each metric.

```{r cv-table}
# per-fold values of one metric, one column per model
fold_values <- function(metric) {
  v <- results_cv$values[, grep(paste0("~", metric, "$"), names(results_cv$values))]
  names(v) <- sub(paste0("~", metric), "", names(v))
  v
}

rmse_folds <- fold_values("RMSE")
r2_folds   <- fold_values("Rsquared")
mae_folds  <- fold_values("MAE")

cv_table <- data.frame(
  model       = unname(model_label[sub("_.*", "", names(rmse_folds))]),
  feature_set = ifelse(names(rmse_folds) == "null", "none", sub(".*_", "", names(rmse_folds))),
  RMSE        = colMeans(rmse_folds),
  RMSE_SD     = apply(rmse_folds, 2, sd),
  Rsquared    = colMeans(r2_folds),      # NA for the null model: its predictions do not vary
  Rsquared_SD = apply(r2_folds, 2, sd),
  MAE         = colMeans(mae_folds),
  MAE_SD      = apply(mae_folds, 2, sd),
  row.names   = NULL) %>%
  arrange(RMSE)

cv_table %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

```{r cv-dotplot, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Cross-validated RMSE by model, with 95% confidence intervals across folds."}
dotplot(results_cv, metric = "RMSE")
```

```{r cv-plot, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Cross-validated RMSE per fold, by model and feature set. Each line is one fold."}
# one row per fold and model, for the plot and the saved results
cv_long <- data.frame(fold = results_cv$values$Resample, rmse_folds, check.names = FALSE) %>%
  pivot_longer(-fold, names_to = "key", values_to = "RMSE") %>%
  mutate(model       = unname(model_label[sub("_.*", "", key)]),
         feature_set = ifelse(key == "null", "none", sub(".*_", "", key)))

cv_long %>%
  filter(key != "null") %>%
  ggplot(aes(feature_set, RMSE, group = fold)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "Feature set", y = "Fold RMSE")
```

### Did the unsupervised features help? Set A versus set B, fold by fold

The same folds scored both feature sets, so the fair comparison is within
each fold. For each model, the difference is set A's fold RMSE minus set B's
on the same fold, as in the course walkthrough:

- **A positive difference means set B did better** (lower RMSE) on that
  fold.
- The difference counts as **larger than the fold-to-fold variability** if
  its mean is more than two standard errors from zero. The standard error is
  the SD of the `r n_folds` fold differences divided by the square root of
  `r n_folds`.

```{r a-vs-b}
# each fit's fold RMSEs, in fold order
fold_rmse <- function(fit) fit$resample[order(fit$resample$Resample), "RMSE"]

# A minus B on each fold
ab <- data.frame(
  fold   = sort(fit_glmnet_A$resample$Resample),
  glmnet = fold_rmse(fit_glmnet_A) - fold_rmse(fit_glmnet_B),
  rf     = fold_rmse(fit_rf_A)     - fold_rmse(fit_rf_B))

ab %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

# mean difference (A minus B), its spread across folds, and the 2 SE rule
diffs  <- ab[-1]
a_vs_b <- data.frame(
  model          = unname(model_label[names(diffs)]),
  RMSE_A         = sapply(names(diffs), function(m) mean(fold_rmse(fits[[paste0(m, "_A")]]))),
  RMSE_B         = sapply(names(diffs), function(m) mean(fold_rmse(fits[[paste0(m, "_B")]]))),
  A_minus_B      = colMeans(diffs),
  sd_diff        = apply(diffs, 2, sd),
  two_SE         = 2 * apply(diffs, 2, sd) / sqrt(nrow(diffs)),
  folds_B_better = colSums(diffs > 0),
  row.names      = NULL)
a_vs_b$beyond_noise <- abs(a_vs_b$A_minus_B) > a_vs_b$two_SE

a_vs_b %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

### Checking the cluster and component choices

The number of clusters and the number of components were chosen in Section 6
from the elbow, the silhouette, and the eigenvalue rules. This section checks
those choices against the alternatives: K = 2 and K = 4 clusters, and one or
three components. Everything here uses the training days and the same
`r n_folds` folds. The test set is not touched.

Each check refits the final model type, the elastic net on set B, with one
piece of set B swapped and everything else held fixed.

```{r check-setup}
# set B with one piece swapped; NULL leaves that piece out
set_B_variant <- function(types = train$play_day_type,
                          needs_block = train[comp_names]) {
  d <- train[c("life_satisfaction", shared)]
  if (!is.null(needs_block)) d <- bind_cols(d, needs_block)
  if (!is.null(types)) d$play_day_type <- types
  d
}

# the same recipe, grid, folds, and seed as fit_glmnet_B
fit_glmnet_check <- function(name, d) {
  fit_or_load(name, {
    r <- recipe_linear(d)
    b <- bake(prep(r), new_data = NULL)
    set.seed(559)
    train(r, data = d, method = "glmnet", trControl = ctrl,
          tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
                                 lambda = lambda_grid(b)))
  })
}

# fold-by-fold comparison with the chosen version, read like A minus B:
# chosen minus variant on each fold, so positive = the variant did better
check_table <- function(fit_list, chosen) {
  ref <- fold_rmse(fit_list[[chosen]])
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fit_list), function(n) {
    r <- fold_rmse(fit_list[[n]])
    d <- ref - r
    data.frame(variant = n, RMSE = mean(r),
               Rsquared = mean(fit_list[[n]]$resample$Rsquared),
               chosen_minus_variant = mean(d),
               two_SE = 2 * sd(d) / sqrt(length(d)),
               folds_variant_better = sum(d > 0))
  })) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
}
```

#### Clusters: K = 2, 3, and 4

The K = 2 and K = 4 types are named by rules, like the K = 3 types:

- **K = 2.** The cluster with higher autonomy is the **good play day**, and
  the other is the **bad play day**.
- **K = 4.**
  - The highest relationships mean is the **connected play day**.
  - Of the rest, the lowest autonomy is the **stalled play day**.
  - Of the remaining two, the higher toxicity is the **toxic social play
    day**.
  - The last is the **smooth solo play day**.

```{r check-k-profiles}
name_k2 <- function(prof) {
  ifelse(prof$gaming_autonomy == max(prof$gaming_autonomy),
         "Good play day", "Bad play day")
}
name_k4 <- function(prof) {
  connected <- which.max(prof$gaming_relationships)
  rest      <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(prof)), connected)
  stalled   <- rest[which.min(prof$gaming_autonomy[rest])]
  rest      <- setdiff(rest, stalled)
  toxic     <- rest[which.max(prof$gaming_toxic[rest])]
  nm <- character(nrow(prof))
  nm[c(connected, stalled, toxic, setdiff(rest, toxic))] <-
    c("Connected play day", "Stalled play day", "Toxic social play day",
      "Smooth solo play day")
  nm
}

k_labels <- list(`2` = name_k2(cluster_profile(km_fits[[2]]$cluster)),
                 `3` = cluster_names,
                 `4` = name_k4(cluster_profile(km_fits[[4]]$cluster)))
k_type <- function(k) k_labels[[as.character(k)]][km_fits[[k]]$cluster]

k_profiles <- bind_rows(lapply(2:4, function(k) {
  cl <- km_fits[[k]]$cluster
  cluster_profile(cl) %>%
    mutate(K = k, type = k_labels[[as.character(k)]][cluster],
           pct_days = round(100 * days / sum(days)),
           mean_life_sat = round(as.numeric(tapply(train$life_satisfaction, cl, mean)), 1)) %>%
    select(K, type, days, pct_days, mean_life_sat, all_of(bangs))
}))
k_profiles

# how each solution splits the one before it (training days)
table(K2 = k_type(2), K3 = k_type(3))
table(K3 = k_type(3), K4 = k_type(4))
```

```{r check-k-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "Cluster centroids on the six BANGS items for K = 2, 3, and 4 (z scores, training days)."}
bind_rows(lapply(2:4, function(k) {
  as.data.frame(km_fits[[k]]$centers) %>%
    mutate(K = paste("K =", k),
           type = paste0(k_labels[[as.character(k)]], "\n(", km_fits[[k]]$size, " days)"))
})) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(bangs), names_to = "item", values_to = "z") %>%
  mutate(item = factor(sub("gaming_", "", item),
                       levels = rev(sub("gaming_", "", bangs)))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(z, item, fill = z > 0)) +
  geom_col() + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ K + type, ncol = 4, labeller = label_wrap_gen(multi_line = FALSE)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#b2182b", "#2166ac"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Cluster mean (z score)", y = NULL)
```

**Stability.** A real type should come back when the data change a little.
K-means is refit on 20 random samples of 80% of the training people. All
training days are then assigned to the nearest centroid of that fit and
compared with the full solution by the adjusted Rand index (1 = the same
partition, 0 = chance agreement).

```{r check-k-stability}
adjusted_rand <- function(a, b) {
  tab <- table(a, b)
  n   <- sum(tab)
  s   <- sum(choose(tab, 2))
  sa  <- sum(choose(rowSums(tab), 2))
  sb  <- sum(choose(colSums(tab), 2))
  expected <- sa * sb / choose(n, 2)
  (s - expected) / ((sa + sb) / 2 - expected)
}

train_people <- unique(train$id)
set.seed(559)
k_stability <- sapply(2:4, function(k) {
  replicate(20, {
    keep <- train$id %in% sample(train_people, round(0.8 * length(train_people)))
    sub_fit <- kmeans(train_bangs[keep, ], centers = k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 50)
    adjusted_rand(nearest_centroid(train_bangs, sub_fit$centers), km_fits[[k]]$cluster)
  })
})
colnames(k_stability) <- paste0("K", 2:4)

k_stability_table <- data.frame(
  K = 2:4,
  silhouette = round(k_choice$silhouette[2:4], 3),
  wss_share_of_k1 = round(k_choice$wss[2:4] / k_choice$wss[1], 3),
  stability_mean = round(colMeans(k_stability), 3),
  stability_min  = round(apply(k_stability, 2, min), 3),
  life_sat_r2 = round(sapply(2:4, function(k)
    summary(lm(train$life_satisfaction ~ factor(km_fits[[k]]$cluster)))$r.squared), 3))
k_stability_table
```

**Prediction.** The elastic net on set B with the play-day type from each K,
and without it:

```{r check-k-fits}
check_k_fits <- list(
  no_play_day_type = fit_glmnet_check("check_no_type", set_B_variant(types = NULL)),
  K2              = fit_glmnet_check("check_K2", set_B_variant(types = factor(k_type(2)))),
  K3_chosen       = fit_glmnet_B,
  K4              = fit_glmnet_check("check_K4", set_B_variant(types = factor(k_type(4)))))

check_k_table <- check_table(check_k_fits, "K3_chosen")
check_k_table

# the play-day-type coefficients the elastic net kept (standardized dummies)
type_coefs <- lapply(check_k_fits[-1], function(f) {
  cf <- as.matrix(coef(f$finalModel, f$bestTune$lambda))
  round(cf[grep("^play_day_type", rownames(cf)), 1], 2)
})
type_coefs
```

**What the check shows.**

- **K = 2** separates good play days from bad ones. It has the highest
  silhouette (`r k_stability_table$silhouette[1]`), but it hides the
  difference between connected and solo play. K = 3 recovers that
  difference, and the two good types differ in life satisfaction.
- **K = 4** is a finer cut. It splits the frustrating play days into a
  **toxic social** type and a **stalled** type. These are the days with the
  "toxic competitive" and "low improvement" sessions the proposal expected.
  It also moves some connected play days into the toxic social type. The criteria do
  not support the extra split:
  - the silhouette is no better (`r k_stability_table$silhouette[3]` against
    `r k_stability_table$silhouette[2]` at K = 3);
  - the solution is less stable (mean adjusted Rand
    `r k_stability_table$stability_mean[3]` against
    `r k_stability_table$stability_mean[2]`);
  - it explains little more of life satisfaction (R² =
    `r k_stability_table$life_sat_r2[3]` against
    `r k_stability_table$life_sat_r2[2]`).
- **K = 3 is kept.** It is as stable as K = 2 (mean adjusted Rand
  `r sprintf("%.3f", k_stability_table$stability_mean[2])` against
  `r sprintf("%.3f", k_stability_table$stability_mean[1])`), it sits at the elbow, and its
  types are distinct enough to name.
- **The number of clusters does not change prediction.** Every version is
  within `r max(abs(check_k_table$chosen_minus_variant))` RMSE of the chosen one,
  and the largest two-SE band is `r max(check_k_table$two_SE)`. Dropping the
  play-day type entirely changes nothing either. The clusters are built from
  the six BANGS items, and set B already contains those items. So the
  play-day type describes the days but gives the model nothing new.

#### Components: one, two, or three

```{r check-pc-solutions}
# scores for m components, built the same way as the chosen two:
# standardized, varimax-rotated when m > 1, and flipped so the strongest
# loading is positive
pca_alternative <- function(m) {
  L <- pca$rotation[, 1:m, drop = FALSE] %*% diag(pca$sdev[1:m], m)
  rotmat <- diag(m)
  if (m > 1) {
    v <- varimax(L)
    L <- unclass(v$loadings)
    rotmat <- v$rotmat
  }
  fl <- sign(apply(L, 2, function(l) l[which.max(abs(l))]))
  L  <- sweep(L, 2, fl, "*")
  colnames(L) <- paste0("C", 1:m)
  sc <- sweep(predict(pca, newdata = train_needs)[, 1:m, drop = FALSE],
              2, pca$sdev[1:m], "/")
  sc <- sweep(sc %*% rotmat, 2, fl, "*")
  colnames(sc) <- colnames(L)
  list(loadings = L, scores = as.data.frame(sc), communality = rowSums(L^2))
}

pc_alt <- lapply(1:3, pca_alternative)

# loadings of the one- and three-component solutions
round(pc_alt[[1]]$loadings, 2)
round(pc_alt[[3]]$loadings, 2)

# share of each item's variance the retained components carry
pc_communality <- round(sapply(pc_alt, `[[`, "communality"), 2)
colnames(pc_communality) <- paste(1:3, "comp.")
pc_communality
```

```{r check-pc-fits}
check_pc_fits <- list(
  one_component          = fit_glmnet_check("check_PC1", set_B_variant(needs_block = pc_alt[[1]]$scores)),
  two_components_chosen  = fit_glmnet_B,
  three_components       = fit_glmnet_check("check_PC3", set_B_variant(needs_block = pc_alt[[3]]$scores)),
  six_needs_items        = fit_glmnet_check("check_raw_needs", set_B_variant(needs_block = train[needs])),
  no_needs_items         = fit_glmnet_check("check_no_needs", set_B_variant(needs_block = NULL)))

check_pc_table <- check_table(check_pc_fits, "two_components_chosen")
check_pc_table
```

**What the check shows.**

- **One component loses information about frustration.** It carries only
  `r round(100 * pc_communality["needs_autonomy_frustrated", 1])`% of the
  variance in autonomy frustration, against
  `r round(100 * pc_communality["needs_autonomy_frustrated", 2])`% with two.
- **Two components predict better than one.** The one-component model's
  RMSE is `r -check_pc_table$chosen_minus_variant[1]` higher, with a two-SE band
  of `r check_pc_table$two_SE[1]`. Two components did better in
  `r n_folds - check_pc_table$folds_variant_better[1]` of the `r n_folds` folds. The gain
  is small, but it is consistent and larger than the fold-to-fold noise.
- **Three components and the six raw items add nothing.** Both are within
  noise of the two components. Two scores carry what the six items carry.
- **The needs block matters.** Without it, the cross-validated R² falls from
  `r check_pc_table$Rsquared[2]` to `r check_pc_table$Rsquared[5]`.
- **Two components are kept.** The scree plot, the eigenvalue rule at 1,
  and parallel analysis favor one, and the 80% rule favors three. The walkthrough's eigenvalue
  cutoff, self-determination theory's split of satisfaction from
  frustration, and this check all favor two.

### Choosing the final model

The rule:

1. Take the model with the lowest mean cross-validated RMSE.
2. If a simpler model is within two standard errors of it, fold by fold, take
   the simpler model instead. The elastic net is simpler than the random
   forest, and set B (fewer columns) is simpler than set A.

The rule was set before the test set was opened.

```{r choose-final}
complexity <- c(glmnet_B = 1, glmnet_A = 2, rf_B = 3, rf_A = 4)
cand <- names(complexity)

mean_rmse <- sapply(cand, function(k) mean(fold_rmse(fits[[k]])))
best <- names(which.min(mean_rmse))

# how far each model's RMSE is above the best one's, fold by fold
# (zero for the best model itself), and the 2 SE of those differences
above_best <- sapply(cand, function(k) {
  d <- fold_rmse(fits[[k]]) - fold_rmse(fits[[best]])
  c(diff = mean(d), two_SE = 2 * sd(d) / sqrt(length(d)))
})
within_noise <- cand[above_best["diff", ] <= above_best["two_SE", ]]
final_key <- within_noise[which.min(complexity[within_noise])]

data.frame(model = cand, mean_RMSE = round(mean_rmse, 3),
           RMSE_above_best = round(above_best["diff", ], 3),
           two_SE = round(above_best["two_SE", ], 3),
           within_noise = cand %in% within_noise, row.names = NULL)

c(lowest_RMSE = best, final_model = final_key)
final_fit <- fits[[final_key]]
```

The final model is the
**`r model_label[[sub("_.*", "", final_key)]]` on feature set
`r sub(".*_", "", final_key)`**.

### The final model's coefficients (training fit)

The recipe standardizes every column, including the dummy columns. So each
coefficient is the change in life satisfaction (0 to 100) for one standard
deviation of that column, with every other predictor held fixed. A
coefficient of zero means the penalty dropped that column (its lasso part,
since `alpha` = `r final_fit$bestTune$alpha`).

```{r final-coefs, eval = grepl("^glmnet", final_key)}
cf <- as.matrix(coef(final_fit$finalModel, final_fit$bestTune$lambda))[, 1]
final_coefs <- data.frame(predictor = names(cf), coef = unname(cf)) %>%
  filter(predictor != "(Intercept)")

c(intercept = round(unname(cf["(Intercept)"]), 2),
  nonzero = sum(final_coefs$coef != 0), columns = nrow(final_coefs))

final_coefs %>%
  filter(coef != 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(coef))) %>%
  mutate(coef = round(coef, 2))

# columns the penalty set to zero
final_coefs$predictor[final_coefs$coef == 0]
```

**The worst-stressor columns.** `stress_worst` is an ordered factor, so
`step_dummy()` codes it with polynomial contrasts:

- `stress_worst_1` is a linear trend across None < Not very < Somewhat <
  Very;
- `stress_worst_2` is a quadratic bend;
- `stress_worst_3` is a cubic wiggle.

These three coefficients do not line up with the levels, so the table below
translates them. It predicts one training day four times, changing only the
worst stressor. The model is linear, so the differences are the same for any
day.

```{r stress-levels, eval = grepl("^glmnet", final_key)}
final_train <- if (grepl("_A$", final_key)) train_A else train_B

# a day with no missing values, so the imputation step changes nothing
one_day <- final_train[complete.cases(final_train), ][rep(1, nlevels(train$stress_worst)), ]
one_day$stress_worst <- factor(levels(train$stress_worst),
                               levels = levels(train$stress_worst), ordered = TRUE)
level_pred <- predict(final_fit, newdata = one_day)

stress_level_effects <- train %>%
  filter(!is.na(stress_worst)) %>%
  group_by(stress_worst) %>%
  summarise(days = n(), mean_life_sat = round(mean(life_satisfaction), 1),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(raw_gap_vs_none   = round(mean_life_sat - mean_life_sat[1], 1),
         model_gap_vs_none = round(level_pred - level_pred[1], 1)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
stress_level_effects
```

- **The raw gap** is the difference in mean life satisfaction from days with
  no stressful event.
- **The model gap** is the same difference with every other predictor held
  fixed.
- **The model gap is much smaller.** A day with a very stressful event is
  `r abs(stress_level_effects$raw_gap_vs_none[4])` points lower on average,
  but only `r abs(stress_level_effects$model_gap_vs_none[4])` points lower
  once needs, sleep, and the rest are held fixed. Stressful days also have
  worse needs and sleep, and those predictors take their share.
- **The decline is curved.** A mild stressor barely changes the prediction,
  and the drop grows at "Somewhat" and "Very."

# 9. The Test Set

This section runs once, after the final model was chosen above.

```{r test-eval, eval = run_test_set}
test_final <- if (grepl("_A$", final_key)) test_A else test_B

test_pred <- data.frame(observed  = test_final$life_satisfaction,
                        predicted = predict(final_fit, newdata = test_final))

test_perf <- postResample(test_pred$predicted, test_pred$observed)
null_test <- postResample(rep(mean(train$life_satisfaction), nrow(test_pred)),
                          test_pred$observed)

round(rbind(final_model_test = test_perf,
            final_model_cv   = unlist(getTrainPerf(final_fit)[1:3]),
            null_test        = null_test), 3)

# for scale, as in the walkthrough: the SD of life satisfaction in the test days
round(sd(test_pred$observed), 3)
```

```{r test-plot, eval = run_test_set, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Observed against predicted life satisfaction, test days."}
ggplot(test_pred, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Predicted life satisfaction", y = "Observed life satisfaction")
```

```{r test-folds, eval = run_test_set}
# the final model's cross-validated metrics across the folds, for comparison
final_folds <- final_fit$resample
round(sapply(final_folds[c("RMSE", "Rsquared", "MAE")], range), 3)
```

**The test result.** The final model was run once on the
`r if (run_test_set) format(nrow(test_pred), big.mark = ",")` test days,
from people it never saw in training.

- **RMSE** `r if (run_test_set) round(test_perf[["RMSE"]], 2)` on the test
  days, against `r round(getTrainPerf(final_fit)$TrainRMSE, 2)` in
  cross-validation. **R²**
  `r if (run_test_set) round(test_perf[["Rsquared"]], 3)` against
  `r round(getTrainPerf(final_fit)$TrainRsquared, 3)`, and **MAE**
  `r if (run_test_set) round(test_perf[["MAE"]], 2)` against
  `r round(getTrainPerf(final_fit)$TrainMAE, 2)`.
- All three are inside the range of the `r n_folds` folds (RMSE
  `r paste(round(range(final_fit$resample$RMSE), 2), collapse = " to ")`,
  R² `r paste(round(range(final_fit$resample$Rsquared), 3), collapse = " to ")`).
  The cross-validated estimate held up on new people.
- Predicting the training mean for every test day gives an RMSE of
  `r if (run_test_set) round(null_test[["RMSE"]], 2)` (the SD of life
  satisfaction in the test days is
  `r if (run_test_set) round(sd(test_pred$observed), 2)`). The final model's
  typical error is
  `r if (run_test_set) round(100 * (1 - test_perf[["RMSE"]] / null_test[["RMSE"]]))`%
  smaller.
- A typical error of about
  `r if (run_test_set) round(test_perf[["MAE"]])` points on the 0 to 100
  scale is enough to flag days that are likely to be low. It is too coarse to
  rank two days that are close.

## Variable importance

```{r varimp, eval = run_test_set, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Variable importance of the final model (top 20)."}
vi <- varImp(final_fit)
vi_table <- vi$importance %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("predictor") %>%
  rename(importance = Overall) %>%
  arrange(desc(importance))
head(vi_table, 20) %>% mutate(importance = round(importance, 1))

plot(vi, top = 20)
```

For `glmnet`, `varImp()` is the absolute value of each coefficient, scaled so
the largest is 100. The recipe standardized every numeric predictor, so the
coefficients are comparable.

- The two need components come first:
  `r if (run_test_set) vi_table$predictor[1]` (100) and
  `r if (run_test_set) vi_table$predictor[2]` (`r if (run_test_set) round(vi_table$importance[2])`).
- Next are
  `r if (run_test_set) vi_table$predictor[3]` (`r if (run_test_set) round(vi_table$importance[3])`)
  and the linear trend of the day's worst stressor,
  `r if (run_test_set) vi_table$predictor[4]` (`r if (run_test_set) round(vi_table$importance[4])`).
- Everything else, including every BANGS item and the person
  characteristics, scores below
  `r if (run_test_set) ceiling(vi_table$importance[5])`.

# 10. Compare and Interpret

**Did the unsupervised features help?** Look at the A versus B table in
Section 8:

- For every model, compare `A_minus_B` with `two_SE` (a positive
  `A_minus_B` means set B had the lower RMSE). Set B
  `r if (all(!a_vs_b$beyond_noise)) "was within fold-to-fold noise of set A for every model" else paste0("differed from set A beyond noise for ", paste(a_vs_b$model[a_vs_b$beyond_noise], collapse = ", "))`.
- Set B swaps six needs items for two scores and adds a three-level
  play-day type. Set B matches set A, so the two components carry what the six items
  carry, in a third of the columns.
- The play-day type adds nothing on top of the BANGS items it was built from,
  because both sets keep those items. The check in Section 8 shows the
  elastic net does as well without it, at any K.

**Do the clusters and components mean something for the research question?**

- Need satisfaction is the strongest single correlate of life satisfaction
  in the training days (r =
  `r round(cor(train$need_satisfaction, train$life_satisfaction), 2)`).
- Frustrating play days have the lowest mean life satisfaction.
- The final model leans on the components. Its two largest coefficients
  (Section 8) are need satisfaction
  (`r round(final_coefs$coef[final_coefs$predictor == "need_satisfaction"], 1)`
  points per SD) and need frustration
  (`r round(final_coefs$coef[final_coefs$predictor == "need_frustration"], 1)`).
  The penalty set both play-day-type columns to zero. The variable importance
  in Section 9 shows the same ranking.

**What a model of days can tell the users, and what it cannot.**

- *What it can tell them.* A well-being check-in could combine a few
  in-game questions with a short needs check. It would flag days that are
  likely to be low in life satisfaction for that player. A frustrating
  play day is one marker.
- *What it cannot tell them.* About `r round(100 * icc)`% of the variation
  in life satisfaction is between people. A model of days cannot say which
  players are generally less satisfied with their lives, or why. That
  question needs a model of people, with person-level averages and traits
  as the unit.
- *Same-day caveat.* Because every predictor is from the same day, the model
  describes what goes together. It does not forecast tomorrow.

**Which model to hand over, and what is lost.**

- The final model is the `r model_label[[sub("_.*", "", final_key)]]` on set
  `r sub(".*_", "", final_key)`. It also had the lowest cross-validated RMSE,
  so no accuracy was given up for readability.
- It can be shared as a list of coefficients, with the direction and size of
  every effect. Nothing is lost in interpretability.
- The random forest did slightly worse (best cross-validated RMSE
  `r round(min(cv_table$RMSE[cv_table$model == "Random forest"]), 2)`,
  against `r round(min(cv_table$RMSE), 2)`), and it would give users only
  importance rankings.

results <- list(
  counts = counts, solo_rule = solo_rule, split_sizes = split_sizes, icc = icc, n_folds = n_folds,
  miss_table = miss_table, intake_missing = intake_missing, var_table = var_table,
  k_choice = k_choice, k_final = k_final, cluster_names = cluster_names,
  cluster_profile = cluster_profile(km$cluster), km = km,
  n_comp_rules = n_comp_rules, n_keep = n_keep, loadings = loadings,
  rotated = rotated, comp_names = comp_names,
  k_profiles = k_profiles, k_stability_table = k_stability_table,
  check_k_table = check_k_table, type_coefs = type_coefs,
  pc_communality = pc_communality, check_pc_table = check_pc_table,
  set_A = set_A, set_B = set_B,
  cv_table = cv_table, cv_long = cv_long, ab = ab, a_vs_b = a_vs_b,
  best_tune = lapply(fits, `[[`, "bestTune"),
  edges = lapply(fits[-1], edge_check),
  final_key = final_key)

if (exists("final_coefs")) {
  results$final_coefs <- final_coefs
  results$stress_level_effects <- stress_level_effects
}

if (run_test_set) {
  results$test_perf <- test_perf
  results$null_test <- null_test
  results$test_pred <- test_pred
  results$vi_table  <- vi_table
}

saveRDS(results, out_path("final_results.rds"))

# all models are fit; shut down the parallel workers
stopCluster(cl)
registerDoSEQ()
```
